learning_outcomes.text: Ability to solve mathematical problems that may arise in engineering. Aptitude to apply knowledge on: linear algebra; geometry; differential geometry; differential and integral calculus; differential and partial differential equations; numerical methods; numerical algorithms; statistics and optimization.
Basic knowledge on the use and programming of computers, operating systems, databases and computer programs with application in engineering.
Adopt a responsible, orderly attitude to work and willingness to learn, considering the challenge posed by the necessary continuous training.

Apply the strategies of the scientific methodology: analyze the problematic situation qualitatively and quantitatively, propose hypotheses and solutions using models typical of industrial engineering, electrical, mechanical and industrial electronics and automatic specialties.
Work effectively in a group, integrating capabilities and knowledge to make decisions in the field of industrial engineering, electrical specialty.

Deduce and infer the value of population parameters with an established reliability level using various inductive statistics tools, through the use of commercial scientific software, from information obtained from a significant random sample (simple problems of interest in engineering and applied sciences) using descriptive statistics.
Develop oral and written presentations that critically argue valid conclusions (reasoned and justified), based on efficient management of acquired information, from the results produced.
Plan and develop a simple research project on an engineering problem coherently in a working group (through cooperation).

Defend learning evidence that demonstrates and justifies the acquisition of work strategies and mechanisms, fostering the continuous need for improvement, particularly through the use of computers and ICT.

syllabus_topics: Classification and calculation of descriptive statistics
Main distributions for discrete random variables
Main distributions for continuous random variables
Main distributions of statistics in sampling
Point estimation of a population parameter
Concept of a parametric hypothesis test
Stages of a parametric hypothesis test
Types of errors in a hypothesis test
assessment_rules: For continuous assessment, the final grade is a weighted sum of a written exam (55%), individual practices (25%), and practical computer applications (20%). A minimum score of 40% is required on the final exam, and the overall weighted average must be 50% or higher. If the final exam score is below 40%, the final grade will be 4.5, even if the weighted average exceeds 50%. For final assessment, evaluation consists of a theoretical-practical exam (80%) and a computer tool knowledge test (20%), with the same minimum score and overall average requirements. Students who do not take the final exam will receive a 'No Presented' grade. For the resit (extraordinary) exam, students can maintain their continuous assessment grade if it is 50% or higher; otherwise, they take a final exam with the same weights and minimum requirements as the final assessment.
